reminder: A universal cover of a space is a simply connected space that covers it.
definition: A universal cover of a [connected space](c:connected-space) $X$ is a [covering space](c:covering-space) $p:\tilde X\to X$ whose total space $\tilde X$ is [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space). It exists when $X$ is [locally path connected](c:locally-path-connected-space) and [semi-locally simply connected](c:semi-locally-simply-connected-topological-space), and then it is unique up to isomorphism of covers.
examples: The map $\mathbb R\to S^1$, $t\mapsto e^{2\pi i t}$, is a universal cover of the circle.
The map $\mathbb R^n\to(S^1)^n$ is a universal cover of the torus, and $S^n$ is its own universal cover for $n\ge2$.
Non-example: $z\mapsto z^2$ on $S^1$ is a covering map, but $S^1$ is not simply connected, so this map is not a universal cover.

steps: Take a space $X$ and a universal cover $p:\tilde X\to X$.
By definition, $p$ is a covering map from $\tilde X$ onto $X$.
So $\tilde X$ is a [covering space](c:covering-space) of $X$.
The universal cover adds that $\tilde X$ is simply connected, so it maps onto every other connected cover of $X$.
links.why: Every fact about covering spaces applies to a universal cover, which is the largest connected cover.

reminder: An upper bound of a subset lies above every element of the subset.
definition: Let $(S,\le)$ be a [preorder](c:is-preorder) and let $A$ be a [subset](c:subset) of $S$. An upper bound of $A$ is an [element](c:element) $x\in S$ with $y\le x$ for every $y\in A$.
examples: In $(\mathbb R,\le)$, the numbers $3$, $4$ and $100$ are upper bounds of $\{1,2,3\}$.
In the subsets of a set ordered by inclusion, the union of a family is an upper bound of the family.
In the natural numbers ordered by divisibility, $12$ is an upper bound of $\{3,4\}$.
Non-example: $2$ is not an upper bound of $\{1,2,3\}$ in $\mathbb R$, because $3\le2$ fails.

steps: Take a subset $A$ of a preorder $S$ and the set $U$ of all upper bounds of $A$.
A [least upper bound](c:least-upper-bound) of $A$ is an element of $U$ that lies below every element of $U$.
So every least upper bound is in particular an upper bound of $A$.
The least upper bound adds the condition that no other upper bound is smaller.
links.why: A result about upper bounds applies to suprema, which are the smallest upper bounds.

reminder: An upper triangular matrix has only zeros below its main diagonal.
definition: An upper triangular matrix is a [square matrix](c:square-matrix) $A=(a_{ij})$ with $a_{ij}=0$ whenever $i>j$. Only the diagonal entries and the entries above the diagonal can be nonzero.
examples: Every diagonal matrix, and the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$.
The factor $R$ in a QR decomposition $A=QR$.
Non-example: $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\4&3\end{pmatrix}$ is not upper triangular, because the entry $a_{21}=4$ lies below the diagonal and is not zero.

steps: A [triangular matrix](c:triangular-matrix) is a square matrix with zeros on one side of its main diagonal.
Choose the side below the main diagonal.
A matrix with zeros there is upper triangular, so it is a triangular matrix.
links.why: Facts about triangular matrices apply to the upper case, which fixes the side of the zeros.

steps: Take a [diagonal matrix](c:diagonal-matrix) $D=(d_{ij})$, so $d_{ij}=0$ whenever $i\ne j$.
Then $d_{ij}=0$ in particular whenever $i>j$.
So $D$ is upper triangular.
Upper triangular matrices also allow nonzero entries above the diagonal.
links.why: Every diagonal matrix is upper triangular, so results for upper triangular matrices cover diagonal ones.

reminder: The VC dimension of a family of sets is the size of the largest set that the family shatters.
definition: Let $\mathcal F$ be a [family of sets](c:family-of-sets) on $X$. A [finite set](c:finite-set) $A\subseteq X$ is [shattered](c:shattering) by $\mathcal F$ when every [subset](c:subset) of $A$ has the form $A\cap F$ with $F\in\mathcal F$. The VC dimension of $\mathcal F$ is the largest size of a shattered set, or $\infty$ if arbitrarily large sets are shattered.
examples: Half-lines $(-\infty,a]$ on $\mathbb R$ have VC dimension $1$.
Closed intervals $[a,b]$ on $\mathbb R$ have VC dimension $2$.
The family of all subsets of an $n$-element set has VC dimension $n$.
Non-example: $3$ is not the VC dimension of intervals, because three points $x<y<z$ are not shattered: no interval contains $x$ and $z$ but not $y$.

reminder: A von Neumann algebra is a *-algebra of bounded operators that contains the identity and is closed in the weak operator topology.
definition: A von Neumann algebra on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ is a [*-subalgebra](c:star-algebra) $M$ of the [bounded operators](c:bounded-linear-operator) on $H$ that contains the identity and is closed in the [weak operator topology](c:weak-operator-topology). By the bicommutant theorem, this holds exactly when $M=M''$, where $M'$ is the [commutant](c:commutant) of $M$.
examples: The algebra $B(H)$ of all bounded operators on $H$.
The algebra $L^\infty(X,\mu)$ acting on $L^2(X,\mu)$ by multiplication.
The matrix algebra $M_n(\mathbb C)$ acting on $\mathbb C^n$.
Non-example: the compact operators on an infinite-dimensional $H$ form a norm-closed *-algebra, but it lacks the identity and is not weakly closed, because its weak closure is $B(H)$.

steps: Take a von Neumann algebra $M$ on $H$, a weakly closed *-subalgebra of $B(H)$.
The weak operator topology is coarser than the norm topology, so a weakly closed set is also norm closed.
So $M$ is a norm-closed *-subalgebra of $B(H)$, and every such algebra is a [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra).
The von Neumann algebra adds closure in the weak operator topology and the identity.
links.why: Every theorem about C*-algebras applies to von Neumann algebras, and weak closure adds more.

reminder: A weak solution satisfies a differential equation only in integrated form against test functions.
definition: A weak solution of a [partial differential equation](c:partial-differential-equation) is a function $u$ that satisfies the equation after you multiply it by every [test function](c:test-function), integrate, and move all derivatives onto the test function by integration by parts. For the [conservation law](c:conservation-law) $u_t+f(u)_x=0$, this means $\iint(u\varphi_t+f(u)\varphi_x)\,dx\,dt=0$ for every smooth $\varphi$ with compact support in $\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)$.
examples: Every classical solution of a conservation law is a weak solution, by integration by parts.
For Burgers' equation $u_t+(u^2/2)_x=0$, the step $u=1$ for $x<t/2$ and $u=0$ for $x>t/2$ is a weak solution, although it jumps.
Non-example: the step $u=1$ for $x<t$ and $u=0$ for $x>t$ is not a weak solution of Burgers' equation, because a jump from $1$ to $0$ must move at speed $1/2$.

reminder: The weak topology is the coarsest topology that keeps every continuous linear functional continuous.
definition: Let $E$ be a [topological vector space](c:topological-vector-space) with [dual space](c:dual-space) $E'$ of continuous [linear functionals](c:linear-functional). The weak topology on $E$ is the coarsest [topology](c:topology) in which every $f\in E'$ is continuous. A sequence $x_n$ converges weakly to $x$ exactly when $f(x_n)\to f(x)$ for every $f\in E'$.
examples: On $\mathbb R^n$, the weak topology equals the usual topology.
In $\ell^2$, the unit vectors $e_n$ converge weakly to $0$, but not in norm, because $\|e_n\|=1$.
On a reflexive Banach space, the closed unit ball is compact in the weak topology.
Non-example: the norm topology of $\ell^2$ is not its weak topology, because the open unit ball is norm open but not weakly open.

reminder: The weak-* topology on a dual space is the coarsest topology that makes every evaluation map continuous.
definition: Let $E$ be a [normed space](c:normed-space) with [dual space](c:dual-space) $E'$. The weak-* topology on $E'$ is the coarsest [topology](c:topology) in which every evaluation map $f\mapsto f(x)$ with $x\in E$ is continuous. A sequence $f_n$ converges weak-* to $f$ exactly when $f_n(x)\to f(x)$ for every $x\in E$.
examples: On $\ell^1=(c_0)'$, the unit vectors $e_n$ converge weak-* to $0$, but not in norm.
In $C(K)'$ for a compact space $K$, the Dirac measures $\delta_{x_n}$ converge weak-* to $\delta_x$ when $x_n\to x$.
The closed unit ball of $E'$ is weak-* compact, by the Banach-Alaoglu theorem.
Non-example: for infinite-dimensional $E$, the norm topology of $E'$ is not the weak-* topology, because the closed unit ball is weak-* compact but not norm compact.

reminder: Abel summation assigns to a series the limit of its power series $\sum a_nr^n$ as $r$ increases to $1$.
definition: The Abel sum of a [series](c:series) $\sum_{n\ge0}a_n$ is the [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) $\lim_{r\to1^-}\sum_{n\ge0}a_nr^n$ of the [power series](c:power-series), when this series converges for $0\le r<1$ and the limit exists; this is a [summability method](c:summability-method). The name also covers Abel's partial summation formula $\sum_{k=1}^na_kb_k=A_nb_n-\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}A_k(b_{k+1}-b_k)$ with $A_k=a_1+\dots+a_k$, a discrete integration by parts.
examples: The series $1-1+1-1+\cdots$ has Abel sum $1/2$, because $\sum(-1)^nr^n=1/(1+r)\to1/2$.
Every convergent series has an Abel sum equal to its ordinary sum, by Abel's theorem.
Partial summation with $a_k=1$ and $A_k=k$ gives $\sum_{k=1}^nb_k=nb_n-\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}k(b_{k+1}-b_k)$.
Non-example: the series $1+2+3+\cdots$ has no Abel sum, because $\sum nr^n=r/(1-r)^2$ tends to infinity as $r\to1^-$.

reminder: An abelian extension is a Galois field extension whose Galois group is abelian.
definition: A [field extension](c:field-extension) $L/K$ is abelian when it is a [Galois extension](c:galois-extension) and its [Galois group](c:galois-group) $\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$ is an [abelian group](c:abelian-group).
examples: Every quadratic extension of a field of characteristic not $2$, such as $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)/\mathbb Q$, is abelian with Galois group of order $2$.
The cyclotomic field $\mathbb Q(\zeta_n)/\mathbb Q$ has Galois group $(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^\times$, which is abelian.
Every extension $\mathbb F_{q^n}/\mathbb F_q$ of finite fields is abelian, with cyclic Galois group of order $n$.
Non-example: $\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]{2},\omega)/\mathbb Q$ with $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$ is Galois, but its Galois group is $S_3$, which is not abelian.

steps: A [Galois extension](c:galois-extension) $L/K$ has a Galois group $G$ of automorphisms of $L$ that fix $K$.
Take a Galois extension whose group $G$ is abelian.
It is a Galois extension, so every theorem on Galois extensions applies.
The abelian case adds the condition $\sigma\tau=\tau\sigma$ for all $\sigma,\tau\in G$.
links.why: Galois theory applies to abelian extensions, and every intermediate field is again Galois over the base.

reminder: A measure is absolutely continuous with respect to another when every null set of the second is a null set of the first.
definition:
Let $\mu$ and $
u$ be [measures](c:measure) on the same [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra). The measure $\mu$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $
u$, written $\mu\ll
u$, when $\mu(A)=0$ for every [measurable set](c:measurable-set) $A$ with $
u(A)=0$. If $\mu$ is finite, this is equivalent to: for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ with $\mu(A)<\varepsilon$ whenever $
u(A)<\delta$.
examples: For a non-negative integrable function $f$, the measure $\mu(A)=\int_Af\,d\nu$ satisfies $\mu\ll\nu$.
The standard normal distribution is absolutely continuous with respect to [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure).
Non-example: the [Dirac measure](c:dirac-measure) $\delta_0$ is not absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, because $\delta_0(\{0\})=1$ while $\{0\}$ has Lebesgue measure $0$.

reminder: An absolute value is a multiplicative, subadditive map from a field to the non-negative reals that vanishes only at zero.
definition: An absolute value on a [field](c:field) $K$ is a map $|\cdot|:K\to[0,\infty)$ into the [real numbers](c:real-number) with $|x|=0$ exactly when $x=0$, $|xy|=|x||y|$ and $|x+y|\le|x|+|y|$ for all $x,y\in K$. It makes $d(x,y)=|x-y|$ a metric on $K$.
examples: The usual absolute value $|x|$ on $\mathbb R$, and the modulus $|z|$ on $\mathbb C$.
The $p$-adic absolute value $|x|_p=p^{-v_p(x)}$ on $\mathbb Q$, with $|0|_p=0$.
The trivial absolute value on any field, with $|0|=0$ and $|x|=1$ for $x\ne0$.
Non-example: $x\mapsto x^2$ on $\mathbb R$ is multiplicative but not subadditive, because $(1+1)^2=4$ is larger than $1^2+1^2=2$.

steps: A [norm](c:norm) on a real or complex vector space $V$ is positive definite, homogeneous and subadditive.
Take $V=K$, where $K$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, as a one-dimensional space over itself.
An absolute value on $K$ is positive definite and subadditive, and multiplicativity gives $|ax|=|a||x|$.
So it is a norm on $K$ with $|1|=1$, and the absolute value adds this normalization.
links.why: On the real and complex numbers, the absolute value is the norm of a one-dimensional space.

reminder: The adjoint $T^*$ of an operator $T$ satisfies $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,T^*y\rangle$ for all $x$ and $y$.
definition: Let $T:H\to K$ be a bounded [linear map](c:linear-map) between [Hilbert spaces](c:hilbert-space). Its adjoint is the unique bounded operator $T^*:K\to H$ with $\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H$ for all $x\in H$ and $y\in K$, where the brackets are the [inner products](c:inner-product-space) of $K$ and $H$. For a densely defined unbounded $T$, the adjoint is defined on those $y$ for which $x\mapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle$ is bounded on the domain of $T$.
examples: For a complex matrix $A$, the adjoint is the conjugate transpose $A^*=\overline{A}^{\,T}$.
On $\ell^2$, the right shift has the left shift as its adjoint.
On $L^2$, multiplication by a bounded function $g$ has the adjoint multiplication by $\overline g$.
Non-example: for $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&i\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ the transpose $\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$ is not the adjoint, because the adjoint is $\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\-i&0\end{pmatrix}$.

steps: Take a [self-adjoint operator](c:self-adjoint-operator) $T$ on $H$, so $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y$.
This is the adjoint identity with $T^*=T$.
So $T$ has an adjoint, and that adjoint is $T$ itself.
The self-adjoint case adds the condition $T^*=T$.
links.why: Every operator has an adjoint, and the self-adjoint operators are those that equal it.

steps: Take a [unitary operator](c:unitary-operator) $U:H\to K$, a surjective linear map that preserves inner products.
Then $\langle Ux,y\rangle=\langle x,U^{-1}y\rangle$ for all $x\in H$ and $y\in K$.
So $U$ has an adjoint, and $U^*=U^{-1}$.
The unitary case adds the conditions $U^*U=1$ and $UU^*=1$.
links.why: A unitary operator is an operator whose adjoint is its inverse.

reminder: The adjugate of a square matrix is the transpose of its cofactor matrix.
definition: For a [square matrix](c:square-matrix) $A$ over a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring), the adjugate $\mathrm{adj}(A)$ has entries $\mathrm{adj}(A)_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}\det(A_{ji})$, where $A_{ji}$ is $A$ without row $j$ and column $i$ and $\det$ is the [determinant](c:determinant). It satisfies $A\,\mathrm{adj}(A)=\mathrm{adj}(A)\,A=\det(A)I$, so $\mathrm{adj}(A)=\det(A)A^{-1}$ when $A$ has an [inverse](c:inverse-matrix).
examples: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$, the adjugate is $\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}$.
For a $1\times1$ matrix $A$, the adjugate is the matrix $(1)$, even when $A=(0)$.
Cramer's rule solves $Ax=b$ by $x=\det(A)^{-1}\mathrm{adj}(A)\,b$ when $\det(A)\ne0$.
Non-example: the cofactor matrix of $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$ is $\begin{pmatrix}4&-3\\-2&1\end{pmatrix}$, but the adjugate is its transpose $\begin{pmatrix}4&-2\\-3&1\end{pmatrix}$.

reminder: An affine map $f$ satisfies $f(p+v)=f(p)+L(v)$ for some fixed linear map $L$.
definition: Let $P$ and $Q$ be [affine spaces](c:affine-space) over a [field](c:field) $k$, with [vector spaces](c:vector-space) $V$ and $W$ of translations. A map $f:P\to Q$ is affine when there is a [linear map](c:linear-map) $L:V\to W$ with $f(p+v)=f(p)+L(v)$ for all $p\in P$ and $v\in V$. The map $L$ is then unique, and $f$ preserves affine combinations.
examples: The map $x\mapsto2x+3$ on $\mathbb R$ is affine with linear part $v\mapsto2v$.
Every translation $p\mapsto p+u$ is affine, with the identity as its linear part.
Every linear map is affine, and so is every constant map, which has linear part $0$.
Non-example: $x\mapsto x^2$ on $\mathbb R$ is not affine, because $(p+v)^2-p^2=2pv+v^2$ depends on $p$ and is not linear in $v$.

steps: Take a [linear map](c:linear-map) $L:V\to W$ and regard $V$ and $W$ as affine spaces over themselves.
Then $L(p+v)=L(p)+L(v)$ for all $p,v\in V$.
So $L$ is an affine map whose linear part is $L$ itself.
Affine maps also allow a shift, as in $f(x)=L(x)+b$ with $f(0)=b$ not necessarily zero.
links.why: A result about affine maps covers linear maps, and the extra freedom is a translation.

reminder: An algebra of sets is a family of sets that contains the empty set and is closed under complement and union.
definition: An algebra of sets on a set $X$ is a [family of sets](c:family-of-sets) $\mathcal A$ of [subsets](c:subset) of $X$ with $\varnothing\in\mathcal A$, with $X\setminus A\in\mathcal A$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$ (closure under [complement](c:complement)), and with $A\cup B\in\mathcal A$ for all $A,B\in\mathcal A$. It is then closed under intersection and difference, and it contains $X$.
examples: The family of all subsets of $X$.
The finite and cofinite subsets of $\mathbb N$.
The finite unions of intervals of the forms $(a,b]$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(a,\infty)$ in $\mathbb R$, together with $\varnothing$ and $\mathbb R$.
Non-example: the finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ do not form an algebra of sets, because the complement of a finite set is infinite.

steps: Take a [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) $\Sigma$ on $X$, so $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing$ and is closed under complement and countable union.
For $A,B\in\Sigma$, use the countable family $A,B,B,B,\dots$ to get $A\cup B\in\Sigma$.
So $\Sigma$ contains the empty set and is closed under complement and finite union.
Hence $\Sigma$ is an algebra of sets, and the sigma-algebra adds closure under countable unions.
links.why: Every sigma-algebra is an algebra of sets, so results for algebras of sets cover sigma-algebras.

reminder: An algebraic closure of a field $k$ is an algebraically closed extension of $k$ that is algebraic over $k$.
definition: An algebraic closure of a [field](c:field) $k$ is a [field extension](c:field-extension) $K/k$ such that $K$ is an [algebraically closed field](c:algebraically-closed-field) and $K$ is an [algebraic extension](c:algebraic-extension) of $k$. Every field has an algebraic closure, and any two algebraic closures of $k$ are isomorphic over $k$.
examples: $\mathbb C$ is an algebraic closure of $\mathbb R$.
The field $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ of algebraic numbers in $\mathbb C$ is an algebraic closure of $\mathbb Q$.
The union of the fields $\mathbb F_{p^{n!}}$ for $n\ge1$ is an algebraic closure of $\mathbb F_p$.
Non-example: $\mathbb C$ is not an algebraic closure of $\mathbb Q$, because $\pi\in\mathbb C$ is not algebraic over $\mathbb Q$.

steps: Take an algebraic closure $K$ of $k$.
By definition, every nonconstant polynomial over $K$ has a root in $K$.
So $K$ is an [algebraically closed field](c:algebraically-closed-field).
The algebraic closure adds that $K$ is algebraic over $k$, so no smaller field between $k$ and $K$ is algebraically closed.
links.why: An algebraic closure is the smallest algebraically closed field above $k$, so facts about algebraically closed fields apply.

steps: Take an algebraic closure $K$ of $k$.
By definition, each element of $K$ is algebraic over $k$.
So $K/k$ is an [algebraic extension](c:algebraic-extension).
The algebraic closure adds that $K$ is algebraically closed, which fixes $K$ up to isomorphism over $k$.
links.why: Facts about algebraic extensions apply to an algebraic closure, which is the largest one.

reminder: Algebraic K-theory assigns to each ring a sequence of abelian groups $K_n$, which starts with the Grothendieck group of projective modules.
definition: Algebraic K-theory assigns to a [ring](c:ring) $R$ the [abelian groups](c:abelian-group) $K_n(R)$ for $n\ge0$, the homotopy groups of a K-theory space built from the finitely generated [projective modules](c:projective-module) over $R$. The group $K_0(R)$ is the [Grothendieck group](c:grothendieck-group) of these modules under direct sum, and $K_1(R)$ is the abelianization of the stable general linear group $GL(R)$.
examples: For a field $F$, $K_0(F)\cong\mathbb Z$ by dimension and $K_1(F)\cong F^\times$.
$K_0(\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ and $K_1(\mathbb Z)\cong\{\pm1\}$.
For a finite field, Quillen showed that $K_{2i-1}(\mathbb F_q)\cong\mathbb Z/(q^i-1)$ and $K_{2i}(\mathbb F_q)=0$ for $i\ge1$.
Non-example: the group $GL_n(R)$ is not a K-group, because it is not abelian in general, and $K_1(R)$ is only the abelianization of its stable limit.

reminder: A subset is algebraically independent over $K$ when no nonzero polynomial over $K$ vanishes at distinct elements of it.
definition: Let $K\subseteq L$ be [fields](c:field). A [subset](c:subset) $S\subseteq L$ is algebraically independent over $K$ when, for all distinct $s_1,\dots,s_n\in S$, the only [polynomial](c:polynomial) $p\in K[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ with $p(s_1,\dots,s_n)=0$ is $p=0$. A subset that is not algebraically independent is algebraically dependent.
examples: The set $\{\pi\}$ is algebraically independent over $\mathbb Q$, because $\pi$ is transcendental.
The variables $\{x,y\}$ are algebraically independent over $K$ in the field $K(x,y)$.
The empty set is algebraically independent over every subfield.
Non-example: $\{x,x^2\}$ in $K(x)$ is algebraically dependent, because $p(u,v)=v-u^2$ is nonzero and $p(x,x^2)=0$.

steps: Take a [transcendental element](c:transcendental-element) $\alpha\in L$ over $K$ and the set $S=\{\alpha\}$.
A polynomial $p\in K[x]$ with $p(\alpha)=0$ must be the zero polynomial, since $\alpha$ is transcendental.
So $S$ is algebraically independent over $K$, and conversely each independent one-element set gives a transcendental element.
Algebraic independence extends the one-element idea to many elements that satisfy no joint polynomial relation.
links.why: A transcendental element is the one-element case, and larger independent sets lead to transcendence bases.

reminder: An annulus is a space homeomorphic to the region between two concentric circles in the plane.
definition: An open annulus is a space [homeomorphic](c:homeomorphism) to $\{z\in\mathbb C:r<|z|<R\}$ for some $0<r<R<\infty$, hence to the product of the [circle](c:circle) $S^1$ with an open interval. A closed annulus is homeomorphic to $S^1\times[0,1]$.
examples: The ring $\{z\in\mathbb C:1<|z|<2\}$.
The punctured plane $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, which is homeomorphic to $S^1\times\mathbb R$.
The open cylinder $S^1\times(0,1)$.
Non-example: the open disk is not an annulus, because it is simply connected, while an annulus has fundamental group $\mathbb Z$.

steps: An annulus is homeomorphic to an open subset of $\mathbb C$.
Every point of an open subset of $\mathbb C$ has a neighbourhood homeomorphic to an open disk.
So the annulus is locally Euclidean of dimension $2$, and it is Hausdorff and second countable.
So it is a [surface](c:surface), and the annulus adds its shape, with one circular hole.
links.why: Results about surfaces apply to annuli, and the extra shape is one circular hole.

reminder: The antipodal map of a sphere sends each point $x$ to the opposite point $-x$.
definition: The antipodal map of the [unit sphere](c:unit-sphere) $S^n\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is the map $a:S^n\to S^n$ with $a(x)=-x$. It is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) with no fixed point, and it has degree $(-1)^{n+1}$.
examples: On the circle $S^1$, the antipodal map is the rotation by $\pi$.
On $S^2$, the antipodal map sends the north pole to the south pole.
The Borsuk-Ulam theorem says that every continuous $f:S^n\to\mathbb R^n$ has a point $x$ with $f(x)=f(-x)$.
Non-example: the reflection $(x_1,x_2,\dots)\mapsto(-x_1,x_2,\dots)$ is not the antipodal map, because it fixes every point with $x_1=0$.

steps: An [involution](c:involution) is a map $f$ with $f\circ f=\mathrm{id}$.
For the antipodal map, $a(a(x))=-(-x)=x$.
So $a$ is an involution of $S^n$.
The antipodal map adds that it has no fixed point, because $x=-x$ forces $x=0$, which is not on the sphere.
links.why: The antipodal map is an involution without fixed points, so it gives a free action of the group of order $2$.

reminder: Asymptotic notation compares the growth of two functions for large input, with symbols such as $O$, $\Omega$ and $\Theta$.
definition: For [functions](c:function) $f,g$ from the [natural numbers](c:natural-number) to the [real numbers](c:real-number), write $f=O(g)$ when there are constants $C>0$ and $N$ with $|f(n)|\le C|g(n)|$ for all $n\ge N$. Write $f=\Omega(g)$ when $g=O(f)$, write $f=\Theta(g)$ when both hold, and write $f=o(g)$ when $f(n)/g(n)\to0$.
examples: $n\log n=o(n^2)$.
Every constant function is $O(1)$.
Non-example: $n^2$ is not $O(n)$, because $n^2/n=n$ is unbounded.

reminder: An augmenting path is a path along which you can make a matching or a flow larger.
definition: For a [matching](c:matching) $M$ in a [graph](c:graph) $G$, an $M$-augmenting [path](c:path) is a path whose two end vertices are not covered by $M$ and whose edges alternate between edges outside $M$ and edges in $M$. Swapping the roles of its edges gives a matching with one more edge. In a [flow network](c:flow-network), an augmenting path is a path from the source to the sink in the residual graph, along which you can send more flow.
examples: In the path $u-v-w-x$ with $M=\{vw\}$, the three edges form an augmenting path, and swapping them gives the larger matching $\{uv,wx\}$.
An edge $uv$ whose ends are both not covered by $M$ is an augmenting path of length $1$.
In a flow network, a path $s\to a\to t$ with positive residual capacity on both edges is an augmenting path.
Non-example: in the path $u-v-w$ with $M=\{vw\}$, the end vertex $w$ is covered by $M$, so the path is not augmenting.

steps: A [path](c:path) in $G$ is a sequence of distinct vertices in which consecutive vertices share an edge.
Fix a matching $M$ and choose a path whose edges alternate between outside $M$ and inside $M$.
If both end vertices of the path are not covered by $M$, the path is an $M$-augmenting path.
So an augmenting path adds alternation and uncovered end vertices to an ordinary path.
links.why: Every fact about paths applies to augmenting paths, which are paths with extra conditions.

reminder: The barycenter of $k$ points $x_1,\dots,x_k$ is their average $\frac1k\sum x_i$.
definition: The barycenter of points $x_1,\dots,x_k$ in a real [vector space](c:vector-space) is the point $\frac1k(x_1+\dots+x_k)$. For the vertices of a [simplex](c:simplex), it is the point whose barycentric coordinates are all equal to $1/k$.
examples: The midpoint of a segment is the barycenter of its two endpoints.
The barycenter of a triangle with vertices $a,b,c$ is $(a+b+c)/3$, the meeting point of its medians.
The barycenter of the standard $n$-simplex $\Delta^n$ is the point $(\frac1{n+1},\dots,\frac1{n+1})$.
Non-example: the circumcenter of an obtuse triangle is not its barycenter, because it lies outside the triangle while the barycenter lies inside.

reminder: The boundary of a set $S$ consists of the points whose every neighbourhood meets both $S$ and its complement.
definition: Let $S$ be a [subset](c:subset) of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$. The boundary $\partial S$ is the set of points $x\in X$ such that every [open neighbourhood](c:open-neighbourhood) of $x$ meets both $S$ and its complement. Equivalently, $\partial S$ is the [closure](c:closure) of $S$ minus the [interior](c:interior) of $S$.
examples: In $\mathbb R$, the boundary of the interval $(0,1)$ is $\{0,1\}$.
In $\mathbb R^2$, the boundary of the open or closed unit disk is the unit circle.
In $\mathbb R$, the boundary of $\mathbb Q$ is all of $\mathbb R$.
Non-example: the point $1/2$ is not in the boundary of $(0,1)$, because the neighbourhood $(0.4,0.6)$ lies inside the set.

reminder: A Bousfield localization of a model category adds weak equivalences so that a chosen class of maps becomes invertible.
definition: Let $M$ be a [model category](c:model-category) and let $S$ be a class of maps in $M$. A left Bousfield localization of $M$ at $S$ is a model structure $L_SM$ on the same category with the same cofibrations, in which every map of $S$ is a weak equivalence, and the identity $M\to L_SM$ is the universal left Quillen functor with this property. In the [homotopy category](c:homotopy-category) of $L_SM$, every map of $S$ is an isomorphism.
examples: Localizing spaces at the map $S^{n+1}\to*$ gives the $n$th Postnikov section $X\to P_nX$.
Localizing spectra at a homology theory $E$ inverts every $E_*$-equivalence, and for $E=H\mathbb Q$ this is rationalization.
Non-example: passing from $M$ to its homotopy category inverts the weak equivalences, but it gives a plain category with no model structure, so it is not a Bousfield localization.

steps: Take the model category of spectra and a spectrum $E$.
Let $S$ be the class of $E_*$-equivalences, the maps that induce isomorphisms in $E$-homology.
The left Bousfield localization at $S$ makes these maps weak equivalences and keeps the cofibrations.
This is the Bousfield localization of spectra at $E$, so it is the case of spectra with a homology theory.
links.why: A theorem for Bousfield localizations of model categories applies to localization of spectra at a homology theory.

reminder: A cartesian closed category has finite products, and each functor $-\times X$ has a right adjoint, the exponential.
definition: A [category](c:category) is cartesian closed when it has a [terminal object](c:terminal-object), binary [products](c:product-category-theory), and for every object $X$ a right [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) $(-)^X$ to the functor $-\times X$. The object $Y^X$ is the [exponential object](c:exponential-object), with $\mathrm{Hom}(Z\times X,Y)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(Z,Y^X)$ naturally in $Z$.
examples: The category of sets, where $Y^X$ is the set of functions from $X$ to $Y$.
The category of small categories, where $Y^X$ is the functor category.
Every Heyting algebra viewed as a category, where the exponential is the implication $X\Rightarrow Y$.

Non-example: the category of vector spaces over a field has finite products but is not cartesian closed, because $-\times X$ would preserve the initial object $0$, while $0\times X\cong X\ne0$ for $X\ne0$.

steps: Give a category with finite products the monoidal structure $\otimes=\times$, with the terminal object as unit.
Cartesian closure says each functor $-\times X$ has a right adjoint, the exponential $(-)^X$.
This is exactly the condition that the monoidal category $(C,\times,1)$ is closed, with internal hom $[X,Y]=Y^X$.
So a cartesian closed category is the closed monoidal category whose tensor product is the categorical product.
links.why: Results about closed monoidal categories apply to cartesian closed ones, which have the product as tensor.

steps: Take a [topos](c:topos) $\mathcal E$.
A topos has all finite limits, so it has a terminal object and binary products.
A topos is also cartesian closed: each functor $-\times X$ has a right adjoint.
So $\mathcal E$ is a cartesian closed category, and a topos adds a subobject classifier.
links.why: Every topos is cartesian closed, so cartesian closed arguments give results about toposes.

reminder: A category has objects and morphisms, with associative composition and an identity morphism on each object.
definition: A category consists of a class of [objects](c:object), a set of morphisms $\mathrm{Hom}(A,B)$ for each pair of objects, a [composition](c:composition) $g\circ f$ of morphisms $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to C$, and an [identity morphism](c:identity-morphism) $1_A$ for each object $A$. Composition is associative, and $1_B\circ f=f=f\circ1_A$ for every $f:A\to B$.
examples: The category of sets, with functions as morphisms.
A group or monoid $G$ is a category with one object and the elements of $G$ as morphisms.
A preorder is a category with a unique morphism $x\to y$ exactly when $x\le y$.
Non-example: the graph $a\to b\to c$ with only these two arrows is not a category, because it has no identity arrows and no composite arrow $a\to c$.

steps: Take a [monoid](c:monoid) $(M,\cdot,1)$.
Form a category with one object $*$ and with the elements of $M$ as the morphisms $*\to*$.
Let $m\circ n=mn$ and let the identity morphism be $1$.
Associativity and the unit laws of the monoid give the category axioms.
links.why: A monoid is a category with one object, so results on categories cover monoids.

steps: Take a [preorder](c:is-preorder) $(P,\le)$.
Let the elements of $P$ be the objects, with one morphism $x\to y$ when $x\le y$ and none otherwise.
Transitivity of $\le$ gives composition, and reflexivity gives the identity morphisms.
Associativity holds because there is at most one morphism between two objects.
links.why: A preorder is a category with at most one morphism between two objects.

reminder: A central simple algebra over $k$ is a finite-dimensional algebra with center $k$ and no proper nonzero two-sided ideals.
definition: A central simple algebra over a [field](c:field) $k$ is a finite-dimensional [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) $A$ over $k$ whose [center](c:center) is exactly $k\cdot1$ and which is a [simple ring](c:is-simple-ring), that is, $A\ne0$ and its only two-sided ideals are $0$ and $A$.
examples: The matrix algebra $M_n(k)$ over any field $k$.
The quaternions $\mathbb H$ as an algebra over $\mathbb R$.
Every division algebra that is finite-dimensional over its center $k$.
Non-example: $\mathbb C$ is a simple $\mathbb R$-algebra, but its center is $\mathbb C\ne\mathbb R$, so it is not central over $\mathbb R$.

steps: An [Azumaya algebra](c:azumaya-algebra) over a commutative ring $R$ is a finitely generated projective $R$-algebra $A$ with $A\otimes_RA^{op}\to\mathrm{End}_R(A)$ an isomorphism.
Take $R=k$, a field, so projective means free and finitely generated means finite-dimensional.
For a finite-dimensional algebra over a field, that isomorphism holds exactly when $A$ is central and simple.
So an Azumaya algebra over a field is a central simple algebra.
links.why: Results about Azumaya algebras apply over a field, where they become the theory of central simple algebras.

reminder: A ring has characteristic zero when no positive multiple of $1$ is zero.
definition: A [ring](c:ring) $R$ has characteristic zero when $n\cdot1\ne0$ in $R$ for every positive [integer](c:integer) $n$. Equivalently, its [characteristic](c:characteristic) is $0$, so the unique [ring homomorphism](c:ring-homomorphism) $\mathbb Z\to R$ is injective.
examples: The rings $\mathbb Z$, $\mathbb Q$, $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb C$.
Every polynomial ring $R[x]$ over a ring $R$ of characteristic zero.
Non-example: $\mathbb F_p$ has $p\cdot1=0$, so its characteristic is $p$, and $\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$ has characteristic $6$.

steps: The [characteristic](c:characteristic) of a ring $R$ is the non-negative generator of the kernel of $\mathbb Z\to R$.
Take a ring $R$ for which this kernel is $\{0\}$.
Its generator is $0$, so the characteristic of $R$ is $0$.
Characteristic zero is the case with zero kernel, and the other cases give a positive characteristic $n$.
links.why: Characteristic zero is the one value of the characteristic where no multiple of $1$ vanishes.

reminder: The circle integral of $f$ over the circle of radius $R$ about $c$ is $\int_0^{2\pi}f(c+Re^{i\theta})\,iRe^{i\theta}\,d\theta$.
definition: For a continuous function $f$ on the circle $|z-c|=R$ in the plane of [complex numbers](c:complex-number), the circle integral $\oint_{|z-c|=R}f(z)\,dz$ is the [contour integral](c:contour-integral) of $f$ along the positively oriented [circle](c:circle) $\gamma(\theta)=c+Re^{i\theta}$ with $0\le\theta\le2\pi$. It equals $\int_0^{2\pi}f(c+Re^{i\theta})\,iRe^{i\theta}\,d\theta$.
examples: $\oint_{|z|=1}\frac{dz}{z}=2\pi i$.
$\oint_{|z|=1}z^n\,dz=0$ for every integer $n\ne-1$.
For $f$ holomorphic near the closed disk, Cauchy's formula gives $f^{(n)}(c)=\frac{n!}{2\pi i}\oint_{|z-c|=R}\frac{f(z)}{(z-c)^{n+1}}\,dz$.
Non-example: the integral of $1/z$ over only the upper half of the unit circle equals $\pi i$, but it is an arc integral, not a circle integral.

steps: A [contour integral](c:contour-integral) of $f$ along a piecewise smooth path $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ is $\int_a^bf(\gamma(t))\gamma'(t)\,dt$.
Take $\gamma(\theta)=c+Re^{i\theta}$ on $[0,2\pi]$, a smooth closed path around the circle.
Then $\gamma'(\theta)=iRe^{i\theta}$, so the contour integral becomes $\int_0^{2\pi}f(c+Re^{i\theta})\,iRe^{i\theta}\,d\theta$.
So the circle integral is the contour integral along one fixed type of closed path.
links.why: Results about contour integrals apply to circle integrals, and the circle gives a concrete formula.

reminder: A differential form $\omega$ is closed when its exterior derivative $d\omega$ is zero.
definition: A [differential form](c:differential-form) $\omega$ on a [manifold](c:manifold) is closed when $d\omega=0$ for the [de Rham differential](c:de-rham-differential) $d$. Equivalently, $\omega$ lies in the kernel of $d$.
examples: Every exact form $d\eta$ is closed, because $d(d\eta)=0$.
Every top-degree form on a manifold is closed, because there are no forms of higher degree.
On $\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}$, the form $\frac{x\,dy-y\,dx}{x^2+y^2}$ is closed but not exact.
Non-example: $\omega=x\,dy$ on $\mathbb R^2$ is not closed, because $d\omega=dx\wedge dy\ne0$.

reminder: A closed monoidal category is a monoidal category in which tensoring with each object has a right adjoint, the internal hom.
definition: A [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category) $(C,\otimes,I)$ is closed when, for every object $X$, the functor $-\otimes X$ has a right [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) $[X,-]$, the [internal hom](c:internal-hom). Then $\mathrm{Hom}(Z\otimes X,Y)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(Z,[X,Y])$ naturally in $Z$, and in a symmetric monoidal category the left and right versions agree.
examples: Sets with the cartesian product, where $[X,Y]$ is the set of functions $X\to Y$.
Vector spaces with the tensor product, where $[X,Y]$ is the space of linear maps $X\to Y$.
Abelian groups with the tensor product, where $[A,B]=\mathrm{Hom}(A,B)$.

Non-example: sets with disjoint union and unit $\varnothing$ form a monoidal category that is not closed, because $-\sqcup X$ would preserve the initial object $\varnothing$, while $\varnothing\sqcup X=X\ne\varnothing$ for $X\ne\varnothing$.

steps: Take a [cartesian closed category](c:cartesian-closed-category) $C$ and give it the monoidal structure $\otimes=\times$, with the terminal object as unit.
Cartesian closure says each functor $-\times X$ has a right adjoint, the exponential $(-)^X$.
This is exactly the condition that $(C,\times,1)$ is closed, with internal hom $[X,Y]=Y^X$.
So $C$ is a closed monoidal category, and the cartesian case adds that the tensor product is the categorical product.
links.why: A theorem for closed monoidal categories applies to cartesian closed categories, such as sets and spaces of functions.

steps: A [closed category](c:closed-category) has an internal hom functor $[-,-]$ and a unit object $I$ with $[I,Y]\cong Y$, together with coherence maps.
Take a closed monoidal category with its internal hom $[X,Y]$ and its monoidal unit $I$.
The isomorphism $[I,Y]\cong Y$ follows from $I\otimes Z\cong Z$ and the adjunction, and the monoidal structure gives the coherence maps.
So it is a closed category, and the monoidal case adds a tensor product left adjoint to the internal hom.
links.why: Facts about closed categories apply to closed monoidal categories, which also have a tensor product.

reminder: A closed operator has a closed graph: if $x_n\to x$ and $Tx_n\to y$, then $x$ is in the domain and $Tx=y$.
definition: Let $X$ and $Y$ be [Banach spaces](c:banach-space) and let $T:D(T)\to Y$ be a [linear map](c:linear-map) defined on a subspace $D(T)\subseteq X$. The operator $T$ is closed when its graph $\{(x,Tx):x\in D(T)\}$ is a closed subset of $X\times Y$. Equivalently, if $x_n\in D(T)$, $x_n\to x$ and $Tx_n\to y$, then $x\in D(T)$ and $Tx=y$.
examples: Every bounded operator that is defined on all of $X$ is closed.
The derivative $d/dx$ with domain $C^1[0,1]$ in $C[0,1]$ with the sup norm is closed, because uniform limits of $f_n$ and $f_n'$ give a $C^1$ limit.
The adjoint of a densely defined operator is closed, so every self-adjoint operator is closed.
Non-example: $d/dx$ on the polynomials in $C[0,1]$ is not closed, because the Taylor polynomials $p_n$ of $e^x$ have $p_n\to e^x$ and $p_n'\to e^x$ uniformly, but $e^x$ is not a polynomial.

steps: Take a [bounded linear operator](c:bounded-linear-operator) $T:X\to Y$ defined on all of $X$.
Let $x_n\to x$ and $Tx_n\to y$; then $Tx_n\to Tx$ because $T$ is continuous.
Limits in $Y$ are unique, so $Tx=y$, and $x$ lies in the domain $X$.
So $T$ is closed, and closed operators also include unbounded operators with a smaller domain.
links.why: A result for closed operators applies to bounded operators, and it also reaches unbounded ones such as derivatives.

reminder: A closed queueing network is a network of service stations in which a fixed number of jobs circulates and none enters or leaves.
definition: A closed queueing network consists of $J$ service stations, each with a queue and servers, and a fixed number $N$ of jobs. After service at station $i$, a job moves to station $j$ with probability $p_{ij}$, so no job arrives from outside and none leaves. With exponential service times, the state (the number of jobs at each station) is a finite-state [Markov chain](c:markov-chain).
examples: The machine-repair model, in which $N$ machines cycle between a working station and a repair station.
A computer in which a fixed pool of $N$ programs cycles between the processor and the disks.
Non-example: an open network, in which jobs arrive from outside and leave after service, is not closed, because its number of jobs changes.

reminder: The closure of a set is the smallest closed set that contains it.
definition: The closure $\overline S$ of a [subset](c:subset) $S$ of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is the smallest [closed set](c:closed-set) that contains $S$, that is, the intersection of all closed sets that contain $S$. Equivalently, $\overline S$ is the set of points every neighbourhood of which meets $S$.
examples: In $\mathbb R$, the closure of $(0,1)$ is $[0,1]$.
In $\mathbb R$, the closure of $\mathbb Q$ is $\mathbb R$.
A set is closed exactly when it equals its own closure.
Non-example: $[0,2]$ is a closed set that contains $(0,1)$, but it is not the closure of $(0,1)$, because it is not the smallest such set.

reminder: A club set is cofinal and closed under suprema of its subsets.
definition: Let $\alpha$ be a well-ordered set, such as an [ordinal](c:ordinal). A subset $C\subseteq\alpha$ is a club set when it is [cofinal](c:cofinal), meaning each element of $\alpha$ is at most some element of $C$, and when every nonempty subset of $C$ that has a [supremum](c:least-upper-bound) in $\alpha$ has that supremum in $C$. For a [regular](c:is-regular) uncountable cardinal $\kappa$, this means that $C$ is closed and unbounded in $\kappa$.
examples: The whole set $\alpha$ is a club set in itself.
The set of limit ordinals below $\omega_1$ is a club set in $\omega_1$.
For $f:\omega_1\to\omega_1$, the set of ordinals $\gamma$ with $f(\xi)<\gamma$ for all $\xi<\gamma$ is a club set in $\omega_1$.
Non-example: the successor ordinals below $\omega_1$ are cofinal but not closed, because $\omega$ is the supremum of $\{1,2,3,\dots\}$ and is not a successor.

reminder: A Noetherian local ring is Cohen-Macaulay when its depth equals its Krull dimension.
definition: A [local ring](c:local-ring) $(R,\mathfrak m)$ that is [Noetherian](c:noetherian-ring) is Cohen-Macaulay when its [depth](c:depth) equals its [Krull dimension](c:krull-dimension), that is, when $\mathfrak m$ contains a [regular sequence](c:regular-sequence) of length $\dim R$. A Noetherian ring is Cohen-Macaulay when its localization at every maximal ideal is Cohen-Macaulay.
examples: Every regular local ring, such as $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ localized at $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$.
Every Artinian local ring, because depth and dimension are both $0$.
Every one-dimensional Noetherian local domain.
Non-example: $k[x,y]/(x^2,xy)$ localized at $(x,y)$ has dimension $1$ and depth $0$, because the nonzero element $x$ is killed by the maximal ideal.

steps: Take a [regular local ring](c:is-regular-local-ring) $R$ of dimension $d$.
Its maximal ideal is generated by $d$ elements that form a regular sequence, so $\operatorname{depth}R\ge d$.
Depth never exceeds dimension, so $\operatorname{depth}R=\dim R$.
So $R$ is Cohen-Macaulay, and the Cohen-Macaulay case drops the requirement that $\mathfrak m$ is generated by $d$ elements.
links.why: Every regular local ring is Cohen-Macaulay, so results on Cohen-Macaulay rings apply to rings of smooth points.

reminder: In the colex order, a finite set $A$ comes before $B$ when the largest element of $A\triangle B$ lies in $B$.
definition: The colex (colexicographic) order compares finite sets of natural numbers by their largest differing element. For finite sets $A\ne B$, put $A<B$ when $\max(A\triangle B)\in B$, where $A\triangle B$ is the [symmetric difference](c:symmetric-difference). On [finite sets](c:finite-set) with $k$ elements, this is the [lexicographic order](c:lexicographic-order) on the lists of their elements sorted from largest to smallest.
examples: The $2$-element subsets of $\{1,2,3,4\}$ in colex order are $12<13<23<14<24<34$.
$\{1,3\}<\{2,3\}$, because the symmetric difference is $\{1,2\}$ and its largest element $2$ lies in $\{2,3\}$.
Non-example: the lexicographic order puts $14$ before $23$, but the colex order puts $23$ before $14$, so lexicographic order is not colex order.

steps: Take two different finite sets $A$ and $B$ of natural numbers.
Their symmetric difference is finite and not empty, so it has a largest element $m$.
Put $A<B$ if $m\in B$ and $B<A$ if $m\in A$; exactly one of these holds.
This relation is transitive and total, so the colex order is a [total order](c:total-order) on finite sets.
links.why: Every fact about total orders holds for the colex order, which uses the rule of the largest differing element.

reminder: A graph colouring gives each vertex a colour so that adjacent vertices never share a colour.
definition: A colouring of a set $X$ with $k$ colours is a [function](c:function) $c:X\to\{1,\dots,k\}$. A proper colouring of a [graph](c:graph) is a colouring of its vertices in which adjacent vertices get different colours, and the least $k$ for which one exists is the chromatic number.
examples: The cycle $C_4$ has a proper colouring with $2$ colours, by alternating the colours around the cycle.
The complete graph $K_n$ needs $n$ colours.
In Schur's theorem, a colouring $c:\{1,\dots,N\}\to\{1,\dots,k\}$ is any function, and it need not be proper.
Non-example: the triangle $K_3$ has no proper colouring with $2$ colours, because two of its three mutually adjacent vertices must share a colour.

reminder: A combinatorial subspace is the set of words obtained by substituting letters for the variables of one template word.
definition: Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $x_1,\dots,x_m$ be distinct variables not in $A$. A template is a [word](c:word) $w$ of length $n$ over $A\cup\{x_1,\dots,x_m\}$ in which each variable occurs at least once. The combinatorial subspace of dimension $m$ given by $w$ is the set of all words in $A^n$ that replace every occurrence of each $x_i$ by one letter $a_i\in A$, the same letter at all occurrences of $x_i$.
examples: With $A=\{0,1\}$ and $w=x_1x_2x_1$, the subspace of dimension $2$ is $\{000,010,101,111\}$.
With $A=\{0,1,2\}$ and $w=x1x$, the subspace of dimension $1$ is $\{010,111,212\}$.
The whole space $A^n$ is a combinatorial subspace of dimension $n$, given by $w=x_1x_2\cdots x_n$.
Non-example: in $\{0,1\}^2$ the set $\{01,10\}$ is not a combinatorial subspace, because a template with one variable gives $\{00,11\}$, $\{00,10\}$, $\{01,11\}$, $\{00,01\}$ or $\{10,11\}$.

steps: Take a [combinatorial line](c:combinatorial-line) in $A^n$, the set $\{w(a):a\in A\}$ of a word $w$ with one variable $x$ that occurs at least once.
This word $w$ is a template with $m=1$ variable.
Substituting each letter $a\in A$ for $x$ gives exactly the line.
So every line is a combinatorial subspace of dimension $1$, and higher dimensions allow several variables.
links.why: A result for combinatorial subspaces covers combinatorial lines, which are the subspaces of dimension $1$.

reminder: A fact is common knowledge when everyone knows it, everyone knows that everyone knows it, and so on without end.
definition: A fact $E$ is common knowledge among a group of agents when every agent knows $E$, every agent knows that every agent knows $E$, and so on to every finite level. In a model where each agent has an information [partition](c:finpartition) of the states, $E$ is common knowledge at a state $\omega$ when the cell of the finest common coarsening of all the partitions that contains $\omega$ lies inside $E$.
examples: A public announcement in a room where everyone hears it and sees that everyone hears it.
If the finest common coarsening of the partitions is the single cell of all states, then only facts that hold in every state are common knowledge.
Non-example: if two people each learn $E$ in private, then $E$ is mutual knowledge, but neither knows that the other learned it, so it is not common knowledge.

reminder: A diagram commutes when any two paths with the same start and end compose to the same morphism.
definition: A commutative diagram in a [category](c:category) is a [free diagram](c:free-diagram) of objects and morphisms in which any two paths with the same start and end have the same [composition](c:composition). That is, all [parallel morphisms](c:parallel-morphisms) that come from composing along paths of the diagram agree.
examples: A square with $f:A\to B$, $h:A\to C$, $g:B\to D$ and $k:C\to D$ commutes exactly when $g\circ f=k\circ h$.
For a natural transformation $\eta:F\Rightarrow G$ and a morphism $f:X\to Y$, the naturality square commutes: $G(f)\circ\eta_X=\eta_Y\circ F(f)$.

Non-example: in the category of sets, let $A=B=C=D=\mathbb R$ with $f=h=g=\mathrm{id}$ and $k=-\mathrm{id}$; then $g\circ f=\mathrm{id}$ differs from $k\circ h=-\mathrm{id}$, so the square does not commute.

steps: Take a [commutative triangle](c:commutative-triangle) with morphisms $f:A\to B$, $g:B\to C$ and $h:A\to C$ that satisfy $g\circ f=h$.
It is a free diagram with three objects and three morphisms.
The only pair of parallel paths is $g\circ f$ and $h$ from $A$ to $C$, and they agree.
So it is a commutative diagram of the special triangular shape.
links.why: A rule for commutative diagrams of every shape also holds for triangles, which are the smallest useful case.

reminder: The commutator $[x,y]$ measures the failure of $x$ and $y$ to commute.
definition: In a [ring](c:ring) or [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra), the commutator of $x$ and $y$ is $[x,y]=xy-yx$, which is zero exactly when $x$ and $y$ commute. In a [group](c:group), the commutator is $[x,y]=x^{-1}y^{-1}xy$, which is the identity exactly when $x$ and $y$ commute.
examples: For the position and momentum operators of quantum mechanics, $[Q,P]=i\hbar$.
In an abelian group or a commutative ring, every commutator is trivial.
Non-example: the anticommutator $xy+yx$ is not the commutator, because it is symmetric in $x$ and $y$, while $[x,y]=-[y,x]$.

steps: A [Lie bracket](c:lie-bracket) is a bilinear map $[\cdot,\cdot]$ with $[x,x]=0$ that satisfies the Jacobi identity.
Take an associative algebra $A$ and set $[x,y]=xy-yx$.
This is bilinear and gives $[x,x]=0$, and the twelve products of the Jacobi sum cancel in pairs.
So the commutator is a Lie bracket on $A$, and it comes from the product of $A$.
links.why: Every associative algebra is a Lie algebra under the commutator, so Lie theory applies to it.

reminder: A compact convex set contains the segment between any two of its points and is compact.
definition: A compact convex set is a subset $K$ of a [topological vector space](c:topological-vector-space) that is [convex](c:convex-set) and [compact](c:compact-space) in the subspace topology. Convex means that $tx+(1-t)y\in K$ for all $x,y\in K$ and $0\le t\le1$.
examples: The closed unit ball of $\mathbb R^n$, and every closed bounded convex subset of $\mathbb R^n$.
The Hilbert cube $\{x\in\ell^2:|x_n|\le1/n\text{ for all }n\}$ is compact and convex in $\ell^2$.
The closed unit ball of the dual of a Banach space, with the weak-* topology, by the Banach-Alaoglu theorem.
Non-example: the closed unit ball of $\ell^2$ with the norm topology is convex but not compact, because the vectors $e_n$ have no convergent subsequence.

steps: Let $K$ be a compact convex set in a topological vector space $E$.
By definition, $K$ is a [convex set](c:convex-set) in $E$.
So every fact about convex sets applies to $K$.
The compact case adds that $K$ is compact, which lets every continuous real function attain its extreme values on $K$.
links.why: Results about convex sets apply to compact convex sets, and compactness adds existence of extreme values.

reminder: A complete lattice is a poset in which every subset has a join and a meet.
definition: A complete lattice is a [partially ordered set](c:partial-order) in which every subset $S$ has a join $\bigvee S$, its [least upper bound](c:least-upper-bound), and a [meet](c:meet) $\bigwedge S$, its greatest lower bound. In particular, it has a least element and a greatest element, the join and the meet of the empty subset.
examples: The power set of a set $X$ ordered by inclusion, with unions as joins and intersections as meets.
The closed interval $[0,1]$ of real numbers with the usual order.
The subgroups of a group ordered by inclusion.
Non-example: $\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]$ has a least and a greatest element, but $\{q:q^2<1/2\}$ has no supremum in it, so it is not a complete lattice.

steps: Take a complete lattice $L$ and two elements $a,b\in L$.
The subset $\{a,b\}$ has a join and a meet, by completeness.
So $L$ has all binary joins and meets, and $L$ is a [lattice](c:lattice).
Completeness adds joins and meets of infinite subsets and of the empty subset.
links.why: Every fact about lattices applies to complete lattices, which also have joins of all subsets.

steps: Take a [complete Boolean algebra](c:complete-boolean-algebra) $B$.
As an ordered set with all joins and meets, $B$ is a complete lattice.
So $B$ is a complete lattice with extra structure.
The Boolean case adds complements and distributivity.
links.why: Results for complete lattices apply to complete Boolean algebras, such as algebras of measurable sets.

reminder: A continuous symmetry is a family of transformations that depends continuously on parameters and leaves a system unchanged.
definition: A continuous symmetry of a physical system is an [action](c:group-action) of a [Lie group](c:lie-group), or of another group with continuous parameters, on the system's states that leaves its energy function or action unchanged. Each one-parameter subgroup gives transformations that depend continuously on a real parameter and start at the identity.
examples: Rotating all spins of the classical XY model $H=-J\sum\cos(\theta_i-\theta_j)$ by one common angle leaves $H$ unchanged, a $U(1)$ symmetry.
Rotating all spins of the Heisenberg model by an element of $SO(3)$.
Spatial translations of a system whose laws do not depend on position.
Non-example: the spin flip $\sigma\mapsto-\sigma$ of the Ising model is a symmetry, but it belongs to a group of order $2$, so it is not a continuous symmetry.

reminder: The functions $f_n$ converge in measure to $f$ when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, the set where $|f_n-f|>\varepsilon$ has measure tending to zero.
definition: Let $(X,\mu)$ be a [measure space](c:measure-space) and let $f_n$ and $f$ be [measurable functions](c:measurable-function). The sequence $f_n$ converges to $f$ in measure when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, $\mu(\{x:|f_n(x)-f(x)|>\varepsilon\})\to0$ as $n\to\infty$.
examples: Uniform convergence $f_n\to f$ implies convergence in measure.
On $[0,1]$, the typewriter sequence of indicator functions of intervals of length $1/k$ that sweep across $[0,1]$ for $k=1,2,3,\dots$ converges to $0$ in measure, although it converges at no point.
Non-example: on $\mathbb R$ with Lebesgue measure, $f_n=1_{[n,n+1]}$ converges to $0$ at every point, but not in measure, because $\{|f_n|>1/2\}$ has measure $1$ for every $n$.

reminder: The covariance matrix of a random vector has entry $(i,j)$ equal to the covariance of its $i$th and $j$th components.
definition: For a vector $X=(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ of [random variables](c:random-variable) with finite second moments, the covariance [matrix](c:matrix) is $\Sigma=E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T]$, where $\mu=E[X]$ is the [expected value](c:expected-value) of $X$. Its entries are $\Sigma_{ij}=E[(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)]$, and it is symmetric and positive semidefinite.
examples: For independent variables with variance $1$, the covariance matrix is the identity matrix.
For $X=(Z,2Z)$ with $\mathrm{Var}(Z)=1$, the covariance matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$, which has rank $1$.
The multivariate normal distribution $N(\mu,\Sigma)$ is determined by its mean $\mu$ and its covariance matrix $\Sigma$.
Non-example: $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ is not a covariance matrix, because it is not positive semidefinite: it has the eigenvalue $-1$.

steps: Take a [random variable](c:random-variable) $X$ with finite variance.
View $X$ as a vector with one component, so $n=1$.
Its covariance matrix is the $1\times1$ matrix with the single entry $E[(X-\mu)^2]$.
That entry is the variance of $X$, so the covariance matrix collects the variances and covariances of many variables.
links.why: The variance is the one-variable case, and the covariance matrix adds the covariances between variables.

reminder: A vector $v$ is cyclic when the algebra acting on $v$ gives every vector, or a dense set of vectors.
definition: Let an [algebra](c:algebra) $\mathcal A$ act linearly on a [vector space](c:vector-space) $H$. A vector $v\in H$ is cyclic for $\mathcal A$ when $\{av:a\in\mathcal A\}=H$; on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) one usually asks only that this set is dense in $H$.
examples: Every nonzero vector of $\mathbb C^n$ is cyclic for the algebra $M_n(\mathbb C)$ of all matrices.
The constant function $1$ is cyclic in $L^2[0,1]$ for the polynomials acting by multiplication, in the dense sense, by the Weierstrass theorem.
In the [GNS construction](c:gns-construction), the vector that represents the state is cyclic.
Non-example: for the diagonal matrices acting on $\mathbb C^2$, the vector $(1,0)$ is not cyclic, because every $av$ is a multiple of $(1,0)$.
